subject: rla
title: Comparing Two Texts on the Same Topic
objectives: Students will identify the central idea or claim and the purpose of each passage in a pair.
Students will compare the point of view of two authors, including who is speaking and what each author believes about the topic.
Students will compare the kinds and quality of evidence two authors use to support their ideas.
Students will synthesize information from two texts by deciding where the texts agree, disagree, add to each other, or complicate each other.
Students will answer paired-passage questions in GED formats, including “both passages,” “Passage 1 only,” and “how does Passage 2 relate to Passage 1” questions.
teach:
Lesson overview

Week 6 asks learners to hold two texts in mind at once. On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts (RLA) test, some reading sets give two passages on the same topic and ask how they relate: what they share, how their purposes and points of view differ, and whose evidence is stronger. The same thinking drives the extended response, where learners read two arguments and decide which is better supported, so this week is a bridge to Weeks 9 and 10. Tell learners that up front: every skill they practice today will be used again on the essay.

The core routine is simple and repeatable: read each passage on its own first, then compare on four points (claim, purpose, point of view, evidence), then synthesize.

Objectives

  • Identify the central idea or claim and the purpose of each passage.
  • Compare two authors' points of view.
  • Compare the type and quality of evidence in each passage.
  • Synthesize: decide where two texts agree, disagree, add, or complicate.
  • Answer paired-passage questions in GED formats.

Materials

  • Student Lesson (printed or on screen) and this week's Notes sheet
  • Whiteboard or shared screen; two colors of markers or highlighters (one color per passage)
  • Copies of the warm-up texts, the three worked-example pairs, and the guided-practice pair (all included below)
  • A blank comparison chart for each learner (four rows: Claim, Purpose, Point of view, Evidence; two columns: Passage 1, Passage 2)
  • Week 6 practice items (the Slower Streets pair, items 1–6, are used for independent practice)

60-minute timing plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5“Same event, two voices”: a museum announcement and a visitor review
Direct instruction20Read each text alone; compare claim, purpose, point of view, evidence; synthesize with Agree/Disagree/Add/Complicate; three worked examples
Guided practice15Whole-group paired texts on a scooter-share program, four questions
Independent practice15Practice items 1–6 (Slower Streets pair); circulate and coach
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; exit ticket; assign the week's study plan

Warm-up (5 minutes): Same event, two voices

Display both texts. Learners read them and answer the three questions in writing.

Text A (museum announcement): Starting in May, the Lakeview History Museum will offer free admission on the first Sunday of every month. The program is funded by a grant from the Lakeview Community Foundation and is designed to make the museum's exhibits available to families who might not otherwise visit. Regular admission is $14 for adults.

Text B (visitor review): We went on the first free Sunday, and it was packed. The exhibits are great, and my kids loved the old fire engine, but we waited forty minutes just to get through the door. Free is nice. Next time I'd rather pay the $14 and actually see things.

  1. What fact appears in both texts?
  2. What is the purpose of each text?
  3. Does the writer of Text B think the program is a good idea?

Answers: (1) The museum offers free admission on (the first) Sunday, and regular admission is $14. (2) Text A informs readers about a new program; Text B shares a personal experience and an opinion. (3) Mixed: the writer likes the exhibits and says “free is nice,” but would rather pay to avoid the crowd. Point out that question 3 has no one-word answer. Paired-passage questions often reward the learner who notices mixed or partial agreement.

Direct instruction (20 minutes)

Talking point 1: What paired passages are (2 minutes)

Say: “Paired passages are two texts on the same topic, often written by different people for different reasons. One might be a news article and one an opinion piece. One might be a history and one a memoir. The GED wants to know whether you can keep them straight and see how they connect.”

Talking point 2: Read each passage on its own first (3 minutes)

Say: “Do not try to compare while you read the first passage. Read Passage 1, then write a one-line label in the margin: who is writing, what the main point is, and why they wrote it. Then do the same for Passage 2.” Model a label for the warm-up: “A: museum, new free Sundays, inform. B: parent, crowded but good exhibits, share opinion.”

Talking point 3: Compare purpose (3 minutes)

Review the four common purposes: inform (report facts), explain (show how or why), persuade (convince the reader to believe or do something), and narrate or reflect (tell a story or share an experience). Genre is a strong clue: a news report usually informs; an editorial or letter to the editor persuades; a memoir narrates and reflects. Warn learners that a text can inform and lean toward a side. Look at the conclusion: a call to action (“Vote no”) signals persuasion.

Talking point 4: Compare point of view (3 minutes)

Point of view has two parts. Who is speaking? (a reporter, an expert, a worker, a family member; first person “I” or third person) and what does the speaker believe? Also ask what the speaker has at stake. A delivery driver writing about speed limits has a personal interest; that does not make him wrong, but it shapes what he notices. A neutral news report may present several points of view without taking one itself.

Talking point 5: Compare evidence (4 minutes)

Draw a two-column chart on the board: Type of evidence and How strong?

TypeStrong when…Weak when…
Statistics and dataa source is named and the numbers fit the claimno source, or the numbers are stretched to prove more than they show
Expert quotationsthe expert works in that fieldthe “expert” has no real connection to the topic
Personal experience (anecdote)it illustrates a point other evidence also supportsone person's experience is used to prove something about everyone
Examplesthey are typical and relevantthey are rare or off topic

Say: “Notice words like everyone, every, always, and nobody. They often signal a claim bigger than the evidence behind it.”

Talking point 6: Synthesize with ADAC (5 minutes, including the worked examples below)

To synthesize is to combine information from two sources into a new understanding. Teach four ways two texts can relate, using the letters ADAC:

  • Agree: both texts state or support the same point.
  • Disagree: the texts make opposite claims.
  • Add: one text gives information the other does not, without contradicting it.
  • Complicate: one text shows that the other's point is not the whole story (an exception, a limit, a cost).

Worked Example 1: What do both texts support?

Text A (summary of a company report): During a six-month trial, Harlan Logistics moved its office staff to a four-day, 36-hour week with no cut in pay. Sick days fell by 22 percent, and the number of employees who quit dropped from 14 in the previous six months to 5. Managers reported that most projects were finished on schedule.

Text B (letter from a warehouse supervisor at Harlan): The four-day week has been great for the office, and I'm happy for them. But my team runs the loading dock, and trucks arrive six days a week. We can't close on Fridays. If the company wants to keep this program, it needs a plan for workers whose jobs don't fit a four-day schedule.

Question: Which statement is supported by both texts? (a) The four-day week should be ended. (b) The four-day week has worked well for office staff. (c) Every Harlan employee should move to a four-day week. (d) Warehouse workers quit more often than office workers.

Solution. Step 1: Label each text. A: report, trial results, inform. B: supervisor, good for office but not for the dock, persuade (asks for a plan). Step 2: Test each choice against both texts. (a) Neither says end it. (b) Text A gives data showing it worked for office staff; Text B says “great for the office.” Both support it. (c) Text B says the dock cannot close on Fridays, so it disagrees. (d) Neither text compares quit rates by job. Answer: (b). Teaching point: Text B complicates Text A. It agrees about the office but adds a limit the report does not mention.

Worked Example 2: Compare purpose and point of view

Text A (county fact sheet): The Mill Creek Dam was built in 1911 to power a sawmill that closed in 1958. The county plans to remove the dam next summer. Engineers estimate removal will cost $2.1 million, compared with $3.4 million to repair the dam's cracked spillway. Removing the dam will reopen about 12 miles of creek to migrating fish.

Text B (blog post by a local fishing guide): I have guided trips on Mill Creek for twenty years, and I can tell you the dam is a wall across the best water in the county. Every spring I watch fish stack up below it with nowhere to go. Taking it out is the best news this creek has had in a century. Come see the difference for yourself next fall.

Question: How does the purpose of Text B differ from the purpose of Text A?

Solution. Step 1: Genre clues. A fact sheet from the county gives dates, costs, and results in a neutral voice; its purpose is to inform. A blog post by a guide uses “I,” strong language (“a wall across the best water,” “best news”), and an invitation; its purpose is to express support and persuade readers to share his enthusiasm. Step 2: Point of view. Text A is third person and takes no personal stance, although its numbers make removal look sensible. Text B is first person from someone with direct experience and a stake (he guides trips on the creek). Answer: Text A informs readers about the plan and its costs; Text B shares a personal, enthusiastic view to win support for removal. Teaching point: the two texts agree about removal but for different reasons: cost and fish passage in A, personal observation in B.

Worked Example 3: Compare evidence

Text A (library director): Two years ago, the Pine Hollow Library stopped charging late fees. Since then, 1,140 cardholders whose accounts had been blocked for unpaid fines have returned to borrowing, and the share of books returned within a month of the due date has stayed the same, at about 96 percent.

Text B (letter from a resident): Getting rid of late fees was a mistake. Everyone knows that people only return things on time when there's a penalty. My neighbor kept a library book for half a year. Without fines, the shelves will be empty within a year.

Question: Which text uses stronger evidence, and why?

Solution. Step 1: List the evidence in each. A: two specific numbers from the library's own records, measured over two years. B: “everyone knows” (a general claim with no proof), one neighbor's story (an anecdote), and a prediction with no support. Step 2: Judge quality. A's data directly tests B's worry: if fines were needed, the on-time rate should have fallen, but it stayed at about 96 percent. B's single story cannot show what happens across a whole library. Answer: Text A, because it uses specific, relevant data over time, while Text B relies on an unsupported generalization and one anecdote. Teaching point: Text A's evidence contradicts Text B's prediction.

Guided practice (15 minutes)

Read the pair aloud, have learners fill in the comparison chart in pairs, then answer together.

Passage 1 (city transportation report): In its first year, the Eastport scooter-share program recorded 212,000 rides. The average ride was 1.4 miles, and a rider survey found that 31 percent of trips replaced a car trip. The city received 640 complaints, most about scooters left on sidewalks. Beginning next year, riders who leave a scooter outside a marked parking zone will be charged a $10 fee.

Passage 2 (letter to the editor): I use a wheelchair, and twice this month I have had to turn around because a scooter was lying across the sidewalk on Bay Street. The city says the program takes cars off the road, and maybe it does. But a sidewalk that I cannot use is not a small problem. A $10 fee will not fix it. The city should require riders to lock scooters to racks, or it should end the program.

  1. What is the purpose of each passage? Expected: Passage 1 informs readers about the program's first-year results and a new rule. Passage 2 persuades the city to take stronger action.
  2. Find one fact that appears in both passages. Expected: The $10 fee, or that the program reduces car trips (Passage 2 grants this with “maybe it does”), or that scooters are left on sidewalks.
  3. How does Passage 2 relate to the complaint data in Passage 1? Expected: It adds a personal example of the sidewalk problem and complicates the report by showing that, for some people, the problem is serious, not minor.
  4. Does the writer of Passage 2 disagree with everything in Passage 1? Expected: No. The writer accepts that the program may reduce car trips but disagrees that the $10 fee is enough.

Checks for understanding

  • Ask: “Why read each passage alone before comparing?” Expected: So you know each author's main point and purpose and do not mix up who said what.
  • Ask: “An answer choice is true for Passage 1 but never mentioned in Passage 2. Can it be correct for a question about what both passages show?” Expected: No. It must be supported by both.
  • Ask: “What is the difference between add and complicate?” Expected: Add gives new, compatible information; complicate shows a limit, exception, or cost that makes the other text's point less simple.
  • Ask: “Name two signs that evidence might be weak.” Expected: No source; one anecdote used to prove something about everyone; words like “everyone” or “always”; a prediction with no support.
  • Ask: “What genre clues suggest a persuasive purpose?” Expected: Opinion piece or letter, first-person stance, strong language, a call to action.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Mixing up the passages. Learners credit Passage 1 with something Passage 2 said. Fix: Use one highlighter color per passage and write the one-line labels before answering any question.

Choosing a “one passage only” answer for a “both” question. The choice is true, but only for one text. Fix: Teach the two-check rule: point to the line in Passage 1, then point to the line in Passage 2. No line in either one means the choice is wrong.

Assuming the authors disagree about everything. Opposing writers often share facts or goals (both want safe streets). Fix: Ask, “What would both of these writers say yes to?”

Treating a neutral report as an opinion. Quoting a supporter is not the same as being a supporter. Fix: Ask, “Is the writer saying this, or reporting that someone else said it?”

Judging evidence by how much they like it. A moving personal story can feel stronger than a statistic. Fix: Ask, “Does this evidence prove the claim as stated, or only one case of it?”

Differentiation

Support: Shorten the texts to three or four sentences each. Provide the comparison chart with the row labels and sentence starters (“Passage 1 wants readers to…”; “Both passages mention…”). Let learners answer orally before writing. Begin with pairs where the purpose difference is obvious (a news brief and a letter).

Stretch: Have learners write a three-sentence synthesis that uses one detail from each passage and a transition of comparison (similarly, in contrast, however, both). Then ask them to decide which passage is better supported and defend the choice with two pieces of evidence, the same task as the extended response.

How this shows up on the GED

Paired passages appear as two texts on one screen, usually labeled Passage 1 and Passage 2. Pairs can be two informational texts (a report and an editorial), two arguments, or an informational text and a literary one (a history and a memoir). Expect these question formats:

  • Multiple choice: “Which statement is supported by both passages?” “How does the purpose of Passage 2 differ from the purpose of Passage 1?” “How does the information in Passage 1 relate to the author's claim in Passage 2?” “Which detail from Passage 2 complicates a claim in Passage 1?”
  • Drag and drop: sort statements into “Passage 1 only,” “Passage 2 only,” and “Both passages.”
  • Select two: choose two details that appear in one passage but not the other, or two points both authors would accept.
  • Hot spot: click the sentence where an author concedes a point or states a claim.
  • Extended response: analyze two arguments and decide which is better supported. Today's evidence routine is the heart of that task.

Assign this week's Practice GED at the end of the week. When you review it, sort missed reading items into “mixed up the passages,” “one-passage-only answer,” and “evidence judgment” so learners can see their pattern.
student:
Why this skill matters

On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, you will sometimes read two passages about the same topic. One might be a news article and the other an opinion piece. One might be a history and the other a personal memory. The questions ask how the two texts connect: what they share, how they differ, and which one makes a stronger case. This is also the main skill you will use on the extended response, so time spent here pays off twice.

Step 1: Read each passage on its own

Do not compare yet. Read Passage 1 and write a short label in the margin or on scratch paper: Who is writing? What is the main point? Why did they write it? Then do the same for Passage 2.

Label example: P1: reporter, city may lower speed limit, inform. P2: delivery driver, fix dangerous streets instead, persuade.

Step 2: Compare on four points

PointQuestion to ask
Claim or central ideaWhat is each author's main point?
PurposeIs the author trying to inform, explain, persuade, or tell a story and reflect?
Point of viewWho is speaking, what do they believe, and what do they have at stake?
EvidenceWhat kind of support does each author use, and how strong is it?

Purpose clues: News reports and fact sheets usually inform. Editorials and letters usually persuade; look for strong language and a call to action like “Vote no.” Memoirs tell a personal story and reflect on what it meant.

Evidence clues: Data with a named source and quotations from people who know the field are usually strong. One personal story used to prove something about everyone is weak. Watch for words like everyone, always, and nobody.

Step 3: Synthesize with ADAC

To synthesize means to put information from two texts together. Two texts can relate in four ways:

  • Agree: both texts support the same point.
  • Disagree: the texts make opposite claims.
  • Add: one text gives new information that fits with the other.
  • Complicate: one text shows that the other's point is not the whole story.

The two-check rule: If a question asks what both passages show, you must be able to point to a line in Passage 1 and a line in Passage 2. If you can find it in only one, the answer is wrong.

Worked examples

Example 1: What do both texts support?

Text A (animal shelter flyer): Adopting an adult dog from Riverbend Animal Shelter costs $75 and includes vaccines and a microchip. Adult dogs are often already house-trained, and our staff will match you with a dog that fits your schedule.

Text B (veterinarian's advice column): Shelter dogs can make wonderful pets, and adult dogs are often calmer than puppies. Still, plan for costs after adoption. Food, yearly checkups, and supplies usually add several hundred dollars in the first year.

Question: Which statement do both texts support?

  1. Adult shelter dogs can be good pets.
  2. The total first-year cost of a dog is $75.
  3. Puppies are better pets than adult dogs.

Solution: Choice 1 is supported by both: Text A says adult dogs are often house-trained and matched to you; Text B says shelter dogs can make wonderful pets. Choice 2 is wrong because Text B says first-year costs are several hundred dollars; $75 is only the adoption fee. Text B complicates Text A on cost. Choice 3 is the opposite of what Text B says.

Example 2: Compare purpose and point of view

Text A (textbook): The Erie Canal opened in 1825. It linked the Hudson River to Lake Erie and cut the cost of shipping goods between New York City and the Great Lakes region. Towns along its route grew quickly.

Text B (a fictional canal worker's diary, written for this lesson): Walked the towpath twelve hours today behind the mules. My boots are through at the heel. Captain says we will reach Buffalo by Thursday if the locks are clear. At night the lanterns of the other boats look like a little moving town.

Question: How do the purposes and points of view differ?

Solution: Text A is third person and gives facts about the canal's importance; its purpose is to inform. Text B is first person from a worker on the canal; its purpose is to record personal experience. Text B adds what the work felt like, something Text A does not cover.

Example 3: Compare evidence

Text A (grocery chain announcement): Since adding self-checkout lanes at its twelve stores last year, Fresh Way has cut average checkout wait times from 7 minutes to 4 minutes, according to its store records.

Text B (letter from a cashier): Self-checkout is a disaster. Customers hate it. Yesterday a man spent ten minutes fighting with a machine that would not read his coupons.

Question: Which text gives stronger support for its claim?

Solution: Text A gives specific numbers from records across twelve stores over a year. Text B says “customers hate it” with no proof and gives one example. One slow customer does not show what happens to most customers. Text A has stronger support. (Notice that Text A comes from the company, which has a reason to look good. That is worth noticing, but its claim is still specific and measurable.)

Try it

1. Text A (city notice): The Elm Street pool will open on June 1 with new hours: 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily. Text B (resident post): Great news that Elm Street opens June 1, but closing at 8 means my kids still can't swim after my shift ends at 7:30. What fact do both texts share, and what does Text B add?

Show answer

Both say the pool opens June 1 (and Text B agrees it closes at 8). Text B adds that the hours do not work for some working parents. It complicates the notice by showing a limit of the new schedule.

2. A news article quotes a farmer who opposes a new highway. Does that mean the news article opposes the highway? Explain.

Show answer

No. Reporting someone's opinion is not the same as holding it. Check whether the article also presents other views and whether the writer states an opinion directly.

3. Passage 1 says a new bus route “carried 8,000 riders in its first month, according to the transit agency.” Passage 2 says, “Nobody rides that bus. I've seen it go by empty a dozen times.” Which is stronger evidence, and why?

Show answer

Passage 1. It gives a specific number from a named source. Passage 2 uses “nobody” and personal sightings, which cannot show how many people rode the bus over a whole month.

4. One passage is a history of a factory town written by a professor. The other is a memoir by someone who grew up there. Name one likely difference in purpose and one in point of view.

Show answer

Purpose: the history informs or explains; the memoir tells a personal story and reflects on it. Point of view: the history is written from the outside, usually in third person; the memoir is first person from an insider.
post:
Summary of key points

  • Paired passages are two texts on the same topic. Read each one alone first and label it: who is writing, the main point, and the purpose.
  • Compare on four points: claim, purpose (inform, explain, persuade, narrate or reflect), point of view (who is speaking, what they believe, what is at stake), and evidence (type and strength).
  • Strong evidence is specific, relevant, and sourced. Weak evidence includes unsupported generalizations (“everyone knows”) and single anecdotes used to prove something about everyone.
  • Synthesize with ADAC: the texts may Agree, Disagree, Add, or Complicate.
  • For “both passages” questions, use the two-check rule: the answer must be supported in Passage 1 and Passage 2.

Exit ticket

1. What three things should your label for each passage include?

Show answer

Who is writing, the main point, and the purpose.

2. A choice is true according to Passage 2 but is never mentioned in Passage 1. Can it be the answer to “Which idea is supported by both passages”?

Show answer

No. It fails the two-check rule because it is supported by only one passage.

3. What is the difference between add and complicate?

Show answer

Add means one text gives new information that fits with the other. Complicate means one text shows a limit, exception, or cost that makes the other text's point less simple.

4. A letter says, “Everyone in town hates the new parking meters.” What kind of evidence is this, and is it strong?

Show answer

It is an unsupported generalization. It is weak because it gives no survey, numbers, or source and claims to speak for everyone.

5. Name one genre that usually informs and one that usually persuades.

Show answer

Informs: a news report, fact sheet, or textbook. Persuades: an editorial, opinion column, or letter to the editor.

Reflection

  • When you read two texts, which comparison is hardest for you: purpose, point of view, or evidence? Why?
  • Think of a time you heard two different accounts of the same event, at work or at home. How did each person's point of view shape the story?
  • Did a personal story ever convince you more than facts did? Looking back, was that fair?

This week's study plan (20–40 minutes a day)

  • Day 1: Reread the Student Lesson and the Notes sheet. Redo the three worked examples without looking at the solutions.
  • Day 2: Complete practice items 1–6 (Slower Streets). Fill in a comparison chart for the pair first. Check every explanation, even for items you got right.
  • Day 3: Complete practice items 7–12. For the lighthouse pair, write one sentence for each letter of ADAC.
  • Day 4: Find two short texts on the same topic (a news story and a letter to the editor work well). Label each and fill in a comparison chart. Write three sentences that synthesize them.
  • Day 5: Take this week's Practice GED under timed conditions.
  • Day 6: Review every missed item on this week's Practice GED. For each paired-passage miss, decide whether you mixed up the passages, picked a one-passage answer, or misjudged the evidence.

Test-taking strategy: Label before you answer

Before you look at the first question on a paired set, spend thirty seconds writing two short labels on your scratch paper: “P1: who, point, purpose” and “P2: who, point, purpose.” When a question asks about one passage, glance at its label first. When a question asks about both, check each answer choice against both labels before you choose. This small step prevents the most common paired-passage mistake: giving one author credit for the other author's idea.

vocab.def: Two texts on the same topic that are read together and compared.
vocab.example: A news article about a new law and a letter from a citizen who opposes it.

vocab.def: To combine information from two or more sources to form a new, fuller understanding.
vocab.example: Using both a report and a worker's letter to explain how a policy affects different people.

vocab.def: The main point an author wants the reader to accept as true.
vocab.example: The city should spend money on speed humps instead of new signs.

vocab.def: The reason an author writes a text, such as to inform, explain, persuade, or tell a story.
vocab.example: A fact sheet informs; an editorial persuades.

vocab.def: Who is speaking in a text and how that person sees the topic, including beliefs and personal stake.
vocab.example: A first-person memoir by a lighthouse keeper's daughter.

vocab.def: Facts, data, examples, quotations, or experiences an author uses to support a claim.
vocab.example: Crash reports fell from 41 to 27 during the pilot year.

vocab.def: A short personal story used as an example. It can illustrate a point but cannot prove that something is true for everyone.
vocab.example: My neighbor kept a library book for six months.

vocab.def: A broad statement about a whole group. It is unsupported when the author gives no evidence that it is true for the group.
vocab.example: Everyone knows drivers ignore speed limit signs.

vocab.def: A point where an author admits that the other side is right about something.
vocab.example: I'll admit that crashes on the pilot streets went down.

vocab.def: To support or confirm information from another source.
vocab.example: The second article corroborates the first by reporting the same cost.

vocab.def: To state the opposite of, or to show that something is not true.
vocab.example: The library's data contradicts the claim that returns would fall.

vocab.def: To show that a point is not the whole story by adding a limit, exception, or cost.
vocab.example: The supervisor's letter complicates the report by noting the warehouse cannot close on Fridays.

vocab.def: A leaning toward one side that can shape what a writer includes or leaves out.
vocab.example: A company's announcement may highlight only its successes.

notes:
Week 6 RLA Study Sheet: Comparing Two Texts

The routine

  1. Read P1 alone. Label: who, main point, purpose.
  2. Read P2 alone. Label it the same way.
  3. Compare on four points (chart below).
  4. Synthesize with ADAC.
  5. Answer, using the two-check rule for “both” questions.

Purpose and genre clues

  • Inform: news report, fact sheet, textbook
  • Explain: how-to, science or history article
  • Persuade: editorial, letter, speech; strong words, call to action
  • Narrate or reflect: memoir, diary, story; “I,” feelings, scenes

ADAC: how texts relate

  • Agree: both support the same point
  • Disagree: opposite claims
  • Add: new information that fits
  • Complicate: a limit, exception, or cost

Point of view questions

  • Who is speaking? First or third person?
  • Insider or outsider?
  • What does the speaker believe?
  • What is at stake for the speaker?

Comparison chart

PointPassage 1Passage 2
Claim or central idea
Purpose
Point of view
Evidence (type and strength)

Judging evidence

StrongerWeaker
Specific data with a named source“Everyone knows,” “always,” “nobody”
Quotes from people who work in the fieldOne anecdote used to prove something about everyone
Typical, relevant examplesNumbers or predictions with no source

Two-check rule: A “both passages” answer must be supported by a line in Passage 1 and a line in Passage 2.

Traps: giving one author the other's idea; a choice true for only one passage; assuming opposing writers disagree about everything; treating a reporter's quote as the reporter's opinion.

stimuli.title: Paired Passages: Slower Streets
stimuli.html:
Passage 1: Ashford Weighs a 20 mph Limit on Neighborhood Streets

(1) The Ashford City Council will vote next month on whether to lower the speed limit on most residential streets from 30 miles per hour to 20. The change would not affect major roads such as Route 9 or Harbor Avenue, which would keep their current limits. If the measure passes, the city would replace about 2,400 speed limit signs over six months at an estimated cost of $380,000.

(2) The proposal grew out of a one-year pilot program. Beginning last spring, the city posted 20 mph signs in six neighborhoods and tracked what happened. According to a report by the city's traffic engineering office, reported crashes on the pilot streets fell from 41 in the year before the pilot to 27 during the pilot year. Crashes that injured a pedestrian or cyclist fell from 9 to 4. Average driving speeds, measured by roadside sensors, dropped from 27 miles per hour to 24.

(3) Supporters say those numbers point in a clear direction. Traffic safety researchers have long found that the speed of a vehicle strongly affects how badly a person on foot is hurt in a collision; a pedestrian struck at 20 miles per hour is far more likely to survive than one struck at 30. “Three miles per hour doesn't sound like much,” said Dana Okafor, a parent who helped organize residents in one pilot neighborhood. “But on a street full of kids, it's the difference between a close call and a tragedy.”

(4) Not everyone is convinced. The Ashford Business Association has asked the council to delay the vote. In a letter to council members, the association argued that slower limits could lengthen delivery and service routes and that drivers may simply ignore signs that do not match the feel of the road. The association recommended physical changes, such as speed humps and raised crosswalks, on the streets with the most crashes.

(5) City traffic engineer Paul Reyes urged caution in reading the pilot results. “One year is a short window, and six neighborhoods is a small sample,” Reyes said. “Crash numbers bounce around from year to year, so we can't say for sure how much of the drop came from the new limit.” Reyes added that his office would recommend combining lower limits with physical changes on the most dangerous streets, if the council approves funding for both.

(6) Residents can comment on the proposal at a public hearing at City Hall on the evening of March 14 or by writing to the city clerk before that date.

Passage 2: A Driver's View: Fix the Dangerous Streets, Not Every Street

by Marcus Bell

(1) I have driven a delivery van in Ashford for fourteen years. I know which corners hide children chasing a ball, which alleys back onto school bus stops, and which streets turn into racetracks after five o'clock. So when I say that a citywide 20 mph limit is the wrong answer, I am not saying that speeding is fine. I am saying that we should spend our money where the danger actually is.

(2) Supporters of the plan point to the city's pilot program, and I'll admit that crashes on the pilot streets went down, which I'm glad to see. But look closer at the report. Average speeds dropped by only three miles per hour. Drivers did not slow down to 20; they slowed down a little, and then they went back to driving the way the road told them to drive. A wide, straight street with no parked cars feels like a 30 mph street, and a sign will not change that feeling.

(3) Every driver I know thinks the new signs are a waste. On my route, I watch cars pass the 20 mph signs in the pilot zone every single day without touching the brakes. If a rule is going to be broken by nearly everyone, it is not really a rule. It is a decoration.

(4) Meanwhile, the city plans to spend $380,000 on new signs. That money could pay for about sixty speed humps on the streets where kids actually get hurt. Speed humps don't need drivers to agree with them. You either slow down or you rattle your teeth loose. The same goes for raised crosswalks near schools and narrower lanes on the streets that invite speeding.

(5) Slower limits also have a cost that the planners don't count. A few extra minutes on each delivery adds up across a whole day. For drivers like me who are paid by the route, not by the hour, that time comes out of our own pockets. Small businesses that run service vans will pay, too, and they will pass those costs on to customers.

(6) I want my neighbors' children to get home safely as much as anyone on the council does. That is exactly why I am asking the council to vote no on the citywide limit and yes on fixing the streets we already know are dangerous. Put the money into concrete, not into signs.

stimuli.title: Paired Passages: The Last Lighthouse Keepers
stimuli.html:
Passage 1: When the Lights Went Automatic

(1) For most of the nineteenth century, every working lighthouse on the American coast depended on a person. Keepers climbed the tower at dusk to light the lamp, and they stayed awake through the night to keep it burning. They trimmed wicks so the flame would not smoke, polished the great glass lens so its beam would carry for miles, and in many towers wound the clockwork that turned the lens. Each morning, they recorded the weather, the condition of the light, and any passing ships in a logbook.

(2) The work was steady and often lonely. Many stations sat on rocky islands or remote points of land, and keepers frequently lived there with their families. When a keeper died or became ill, a wife or daughter sometimes took over the job, and a number of women were appointed as keepers in their own right.

(3) In the early twentieth century, technology began to change the job. Electric lamps replaced oil, and electric motors replaced hand-wound clockwork. Later, devices that switched a light on at dusk and off at dawn removed the need for anyone to tend the lamp at all. In 1939, responsibility for the nation's lighthouses passed to the U.S. Coast Guard, which gradually converted the stations to automatic operation. By the end of the 1990s, nearly every lighthouse in the country ran without a resident keeper.

(4) The main reasons for the change were cost and reliability. Paying and housing a keeper at a remote station was expensive, and supplying an island station by boat could be difficult in bad weather. Automatic equipment, by contrast, could run for long periods with only occasional visits from maintenance crews. Automated lights are typically equipped with backup batteries and spare lamps that switch on by themselves if the main lamp fails.

(5) Today, many former keepers' houses stand empty or have been turned into museums. The lights themselves still shine, now watched over by sensors and checked by crews who arrive by truck or boat a few times a year. By most measures, automation did what it was meant to do: it kept the lights burning at a fraction of the cost.

Passage 2: The Winter the Light Stopped Needing Us

(1) I was eleven the winter the Coast Guard came to automate the light at Gannet Point. My father had kept that light for nineteen years, and his father had kept it before him. I had never lived anywhere else. Our kitchen window looked straight up at the tower, and I fell asleep most nights counting the slow sweep of the beam across my ceiling: one, two, three, dark.

(2) The technicians arrived in early December with crates of gray equipment. They were polite young men who called my father “sir” and asked him where the fuses were kept. My father showed them everything. He showed them the logbooks, too, forty-one of them on a shelf by the stairs, every one filled in his small, square handwriting or his father's. One of the technicians flipped through a book from 1952 and whistled. “You wrote down every ship?” he asked. “Every one I saw,” my father said.

(3) I remember one night that February, after the new equipment was running but before we had moved out. A storm took down the power line from the mainland, and the backup battery that was supposed to take over did not. The tower went black. My father was up the stairs with a lantern and the old kerosene lamp before I had my boots on. He kept the light going by hand until dawn, and in the morning he wrote it all down in the logbook, the way he always had. Nobody from the Coast Guard ever asked to see that entry.

(4) We left Gannet Point in April. On our last evening, my father stood at the kitchen window and watched the beam come on by itself at dusk. He did not say anything for a long time. Then he said, mostly to himself, “Well. It doesn't need me anymore.” He sounded proud and something else, something I didn't have a word for at eleven.

(5) People tell me automation was the sensible choice, and I believe them. The numbers were on its side. But I also know that for one night in February, the light at Gannet Point stayed lit because a man was awake to climb the stairs.
stimuli.source: Both passages were written for this course. Passage 2 is a work of fiction.

stimuli.title: Draft Response: Two Views on Slower Streets
stimuli.html:
A GED student wrote this draft response comparing the two Slower Streets passages. It contains blanks where the student is deciding between word choices.

(1) Both passages discuss Ashford's plan to lower the speed limit on residential streets to 20 miles per hour. The news article in Passage 1 explains the proposal and reports what people on each side think. (A) the opinion piece in Passage 2 argues against the plan from the point of view of a delivery driver.

(2) The two passages use some of the same evidence. Each of the writers (B) the city's pilot program and the $380,000 cost of new signs. However, they use that evidence differently. Passage 1 reports the numbers and lets the city engineer warn that one year is a short time. Bell uses the same numbers to argue that the signs did not work.

(3) In my view, Passage 1 gives the more reliable picture. Bell's experience as a driver is real, but (C) not enough to prove that nearly every driver ignores the signs. His claim that $380,000 could pay for sixty speed humps also has no source.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of Passage 1?
options: to inform readers about a proposed speed limit change and the views of people for and against it
to persuade the city council to approve the 20 mph limit before the March hearing
to criticize the Ashford Business Association for asking the council to delay the vote
to explain how roadside sensors measure the speed of passing cars
items.hint: Look at the type of text it is and at whose views it reports. Does the writer ever say what the council should do?
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify the genre. Passage 1 is a news article: it gives facts (the vote, the cost, the pilot data) and quotes several people.

Step 2. Check whose views appear. Paragraph 3 presents supporters, paragraph 4 presents the business association's objections, and paragraph 5 presents the engineer's caution. The writer never says what the council should do.

Step 3. A text that reports facts and several sides without taking one is written to inform. The choice about informing readers of the proposed change and the views for and against it is correct.

The “persuade the council” choice confuses quoting a supporter (Dana Okafor) with being a supporter. The “criticize” choice is wrong because the article reports the association's view without judging it. The sensors choice is too narrow; sensors are mentioned once, in paragraph 2.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Marcus Bell's main claim in Passage 2?
options: Speeding on residential streets is not a serious problem in Ashford.
Ashford should spend its money on physical changes to its most dangerous streets instead of a citywide 20 mph limit.
The city's pilot program had no effect on the number of crashes.
Delivery drivers in Ashford should be paid by the hour instead of by the route.
items.hint: Read the last two sentences of paragraph 1 and the request in paragraph 6.
items.explain:
Step 1. Find where Bell states his position. Paragraph 1 ends: “we should spend our money where the danger actually is.” Paragraph 6 asks the council to “vote no on the citywide limit and yes on fixing the streets we already know are dangerous.”

Step 2. Combine those statements: spend on fixing dangerous streets, not on a citywide limit. That matches the choice about spending on physical changes to the most dangerous streets instead of a citywide limit. Correct.

The choice that speeding is not a serious problem is the opposite of what Bell says: “I am not saying that speeding is fine.” The pilot choice contradicts paragraph 2, where Bell admits crashes went down. The pay choice twists a detail from paragraph 5; Bell mentions being paid by the route to show a cost of slower limits, not to argue for a change in pay.

items.prompt: The sentences below are from paragraph 2 of Passage 2. Click the sentence in which Bell concedes (admits) a point that helps the other side of the argument.
spans: Supporters of the plan point to the city's pilot program, and I'll admit that crashes on the pilot streets went down, which I'm glad to see.
But look closer at the report.
Average speeds dropped by only three miles per hour.
Drivers did not slow down to 20; they slowed down a little, and then they went back to driving the way the road told them to drive.
A wide, straight street with no parked cars feels like a 30 mph street, and a sign will not change that feeling.
items.hint: Look for a signal phrase such as “I'll admit” and ask whether the fact it introduces helps supporters of the lower limit.
items.explain:
Step 1. A concession is a point the author admits is true even though it helps the other side.

Step 2. The first sentence uses the signal phrase “I'll admit” and states that crashes on the pilot streets went down. Fewer crashes is the strongest evidence for the lower limit, so admitting it helps the other side. Correct.

Step 3. Check the others. “But look closer at the report” is the turn back to Bell's own argument. The sentence about speeds dropping “only three miles per hour” is a fact Bell uses to support his side; the word “only” shows he is downplaying it. The last two sentences are Bell's own reasoning.

items.prompt: Which statement is supported by information in both passages?
options: The 20 mph limit was the main cause of the drop in crashes on the pilot streets.
Most drivers in the pilot zone did not slow down at all when they passed the new signs.
The number of crashes on the pilot streets went down during the pilot year.
Slower speed limits will raise the prices that Ashford customers pay for services.
items.hint: Use the two-check rule: find a line in Passage 1 and a line in Passage 2 for the same choice.
items.explain:
Step 1. Test each choice in Passage 1, then in Passage 2.

Step 2. Crashes went down: Passage 1, paragraph 2 reports crashes fell from 41 to 27. Passage 2, paragraph 2: “I'll admit that crashes on the pilot streets went down.” Both passages support it. Correct.

Step 3. The other choices fail the two-check rule. “Main cause” is not supported by either passage; in fact, the engineer in Passage 1 says “we can't say for sure how much of the drop came from the new limit.” The claim that drivers “did not slow down at all” appears only in Passage 2 (Bell's observation), and Passage 1's sensor data shows average speeds did drop. Higher prices for customers is Bell's prediction in Passage 2 only.

items.prompt: Select two pieces of information that appear in Passage 1 but are not mentioned in Passage 2.
options: Crashes that injured a pedestrian or cyclist fell from 9 to 4.
The city engineer warned that one year of data is too short to be sure what caused the drop in crashes.
Average driving speeds dropped by about three miles per hour.
Replacing the signs would cost about $380,000.
Speed humps could be used to slow traffic on dangerous streets.
items.hint: For each choice, look for it in Passage 2. If you find it there, cross it out.
items.explain:
Step 1. Confirm every choice appears in Passage 1. All five do: injury crashes (paragraph 2), the engineer's warning (paragraph 5), speeds from 27 to 24 (paragraph 2), $380,000 (paragraph 1), and speed humps (paragraph 4, from the business association, and paragraph 5).

Step 2. Now search Passage 2 for each.

  • Injury crashes falling from 9 to 4: Passage 2 never gives this number. Correct.
  • The engineer's warning: Bell never mentions the engineer or the length of the pilot. Correct.
  • Speeds dropping three miles per hour: Bell says “Average speeds dropped by only three miles per hour” (paragraph 2). Appears in both.
  • $380,000: Bell names this cost in paragraph 4. Appears in both.
  • Speed humps: Bell's main solution in paragraph 4. Appears in both.

Notice that Bell leaves out the two details that would most help the other side: the drop in injury crashes and the engineer's balanced explanation.

items.prompt: Drag each statement into the correct category to show which passage it describes.
choices: Uses the writer's own experience as evidence
Mentions the cost of replacing the signs
Ends with a direct request to the city council
Reports that crashes went down on the pilot streets
Argues that drivers who are paid by the route will lose money
items.hint: Passage 1 is a news report; Passage 2 is a personal opinion piece. Check each statement against both before placing it.
items.explain:
Passage 1 only: “Quotes a city official.” Passage 1 quotes traffic engineer Paul Reyes (paragraph 5). Passage 2 quotes no one.

Passage 2 only: “Uses the writer's own experience” (Bell's fourteen years of driving and what he sees on his route). “Ends with a direct request to the city council” (“I am asking the council to vote no…”); Passage 1 ends with information about the public hearing, not a request. “Drivers who are paid by the route will lose money” (paragraph 5 of Passage 2). Passage 1 mentions that the business association worries about longer routes, but it never mentions drivers being paid by the route.

Both passages: The cost of the signs ($380,000 appears in paragraph 1 of Passage 1 and paragraph 4 of Passage 2) and the drop in crashes (paragraph 2 of each).

items.skill: Transitions of comparison; agreement; confused words
items.prompt:
Read the student's draft response. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 1, blank (A): {{0}} the opinion piece in Passage 2 argues against the plan from the point of view of a delivery driver.

Paragraph 2, blank (B): Each of the writers {{1}} the city's pilot program and the $380,000 cost of new signs.

Paragraph 3, blank (C): Bell's experience as a driver is real, but {{2}} not enough to prove that nearly every driver ignores the signs.

options: In contrast,
Similarly,
For example,
As a result,
mention
mentions
are mentioning
have mentioned
it's
its
its'

items.hint: For (A), ask whether the sentence shows a likeness or a difference from the sentence before it. For (B), find the true subject. For (C), try reading the blank as “it is.”
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: The sentence before says Passage 1 “explains the proposal and reports what people on each side think.” Step 2: This sentence says Passage 2 “argues against the plan.” Explaining both sides and arguing one side are different, so the transition must show contrast: “In contrast,” Correct. “Similarly” signals a likeness, “For example” signals an example of the previous point, and “As a result” signals an effect; none fits.

Blank (B). Step 1: The subject is “Each,” not “writers”; “of the writers” is a phrase that describes it. Step 2: “Each” is singular, and the paragraph is in present tense (“use,” “reports”). Step 3: A singular, present-tense verb is needed: “Each of the writers mentions.” Correct. “Mention,” “are mentioning,” and “have mentioned” are all plural forms.

Blank (C). Step 1: The sentence needs a subject and a verb: “but it is not enough.” Step 2: The contraction of “it is” is “it's.” Correct. “Its” shows ownership (“the dog wagged its tail”) and would leave the clause without a verb. “Its'” is not a word in standard English.

items.prompt: How does the purpose of Passage 2 differ from the purpose of Passage 1?
options: Passage 1 argues that automation was a mistake, while Passage 2 defends the decision to automate.
Passage 1 tells the story of one keeper's family, while Passage 2 gives a general history of American lighthouses.
Passage 1 explains how and why lighthouses across the country were automated, while Passage 2 shares one family's personal experience of that change.
Passage 1 persuades readers to visit lighthouse museums, while Passage 2 persuades readers to become Coast Guard technicians.
items.hint: Label each passage: who is writing, and is the passage about the whole country or one place?
items.explain:
Step 1. Label Passage 1. It is written in third person, covers lighthouses “on the American coast” over more than a century, and gives causes (“The main reasons for the change were cost and reliability”). Its purpose is to inform and explain.

Step 2. Label Passage 2. It is told in first person (“I was eleven”) by a keeper's daughter about one station, Gannet Point, and reflects on what the change meant to her family. Its purpose is to narrate and reflect.

Step 3. The choice that says Passage 1 explains how and why lighthouses were automated while Passage 2 shares one family's experience matches both labels. Correct.

The choice about Passage 1 arguing that automation was a mistake gets both passages wrong: Passage 1 calls automation a success, and Passage 2 does not simply defend it. The choice that gives Passage 1 the family story and Passage 2 the general history swaps the passages. The museum choice is not stated; museums are mentioned once in Passage 1, and neither passage urges readers to do anything.

items.prompt: Which statement best compares the two passages' points of view on automation?
options: Both passages present automation as a loss that should not have happened.
Passage 1 presents automation as a success, while the narrator of Passage 2 accepts that it was sensible but also feels a sense of loss.
Passage 1 is critical of the Coast Guard, while the narrator of Passage 2 praises the Coast Guard technicians.
Passage 1 shows strong personal emotion, while Passage 2 avoids expressing any feelings.
items.hint: Compare the last paragraph of each passage. What does each writer say automation accomplished, and how does the narrator of Passage 2 feel?
items.explain:
Step 1. Passage 1's view: its last sentence says, “By most measures, automation did what it was meant to do: it kept the lights burning at a fraction of the cost.” That presents automation as a success.

Step 2. Passage 2's view: the narrator says, “People tell me automation was the sensible choice, and I believe them.” But she also describes her father sounding “proud and something else” and ends with the night a person had to keep the light lit. She accepts the decision but feels a loss.

Step 3. The choice that says Passage 1 presents automation as a success while the narrator accepts it as sensible but feels a loss captures both views. Correct.

The choice that both passages present automation as a loss is wrong because Passage 1 does not present automation as a loss, and the narrator of Passage 2 says she believes it was sensible. The Coast Guard choice is not supported: Passage 1 simply reports what the Coast Guard did, and Passage 2 describes the technicians as polite but does not praise the Coast Guard. The emotion choice reverses the passages: Passage 2 is the emotional one.

items.prompt: Which statement best compares how the two Slower Streets passages use evidence?
options: Passage 1 relies only on statistics, while Passage 2 relies only on quotations from traffic experts.
Both passages rely mainly on personal stories rather than on data.
Passage 2 uses more reliable evidence than Passage 1 because its writer drives Ashford's streets every day.
Passage 1 relies mainly on data from a city report and quotations from several sources, while Passage 2 relies mainly on the writer's own observations and includes some claims without a source.
items.hint: List the kinds of evidence in each passage. Then look for any claim in Passage 2 that has no source.
items.explain:
Step 1. List Passage 1's evidence: crash and speed numbers from the city's traffic engineering report (paragraph 2), a research finding about pedestrian survival (paragraph 3), and quotations from a parent, the business association, and the city engineer (paragraphs 3–5).

Step 2. List Passage 2's evidence: Bell's fourteen years of driving and what he sees on his route (paragraphs 1 and 3), one number taken from the city report (the three-mile-per-hour drop), and claims with no source: “Every driver I know thinks the new signs are a waste” (an unsupported generalization) and “That money could pay for about sixty speed humps” (no source given).

Step 3. The choice that says Passage 1 relies on a city report and several sources while Passage 2 relies on the writer's observations and some unsourced claims matches both lists. Correct.

The choice that Passage 1 uses only statistics and Passage 2 only expert quotations is wrong twice: Passage 1 also uses quotations, and Passage 2 quotes no experts. The choice that both passages rely mainly on personal stories is wrong because Passage 1 is built on data. The choice that Passage 2 is more reliable because its writer drives every day is the trap of judging evidence by the writer's experience; daily observation by one driver cannot show what drivers across the pilot zone did, which is what the sensor data measures.

items.skill: Synthesis: how one text relates to another
items.prompt: How does the information in paragraph 5 of Passage 1 relate to Bell's argument in Passage 2?
options: It fully supports Bell, because the engineer recommends that the council reject the lower limit.

It partly supports Bell, because the engineer doubts that the limit alone explains the drop in crashes and favors physical changes on dangerous streets, but he recommends using those changes together with lower limits.
It contradicts Bell, because the engineer says the lower limit was the main cause of the drop in crashes.
It has no connection to Bell's argument, because the engineer discusses only the cost of the new signs.
items.hint: Reread paragraph 5 sentence by sentence. Which parts would Bell agree with? Is there any part he would not?
items.explain:
Step 1. Summarize paragraph 5. The engineer says one year and six neighborhoods are too little data to know “how much of the drop came from the new limit.” He would recommend “combining lower limits with physical changes on the most dangerous streets.”

Step 2. Compare with Bell. Bell doubts that the signs work and wants physical changes on dangerous streets. The engineer's doubt and his support for physical changes agree with Bell. But the engineer wants lower limits too, while Bell asks the council to vote no on the limit. So the paragraph partly supports Bell and partly complicates his argument.

Step 3. The choice that says paragraph 5 partly supports Bell describes this mixed relationship. Correct.

The “fully supports” choice is wrong because the engineer never recommends rejecting the limit. The “contradicts” choice is wrong because the engineer says the opposite: “we can't say for sure.” The “no connection” choice is wrong because paragraph 5 does not discuss sign costs at all.

items.skill: Synthesis: how one text complicates another
items.prompt: How does the event described in paragraph 3 of Passage 2 complicate a claim made in Passage 1?
options: Passage 1 says keepers stayed awake through the night, but Passage 2 shows that the narrator's father slept through the storm.
Passage 1 says the Coast Guard took over the nation's lighthouses in 1939, but Passage 2 shows that the Coast Guard never came to Gannet Point.
Passage 1 says automated lights have backup systems that switch on by themselves, but in Passage 2 the backup battery failed and a person had to keep the light going.
Passage 1 says keepers recorded events in logbooks, but Passage 2 shows that the narrator's father stopped keeping a logbook once the light was automated.
items.hint: First, summarize what happens in paragraph 3 of Passage 2. Then find the sentence in Passage 1 that the event challenges.
items.explain:
Step 1. Summarize paragraph 3 of Passage 2: a storm cut the power, “the backup battery that was supposed to take over did not,” and the father kept the light going by hand until dawn.

Step 2. Find the related claim in Passage 1. Paragraph 4 says automated lights have “backup batteries and spare lamps that switch on by themselves if the main lamp fails.”

Step 3. The memoir shows a case where that backup did not work and a human was needed. It does not prove Passage 1 wrong in general, but it shows the claim is not the whole story. That is what complicate means. The choice about the failed backup battery and the person who kept the light going is correct.

The other choices misstate Passage 2. The father did not sleep; he “was up the stairs with a lantern.” The Coast Guard did come; its technicians installed the equipment in December. The father did not stop his logbook; “in the morning he wrote it all down in the logbook, the way he always had.”
